Sources

Geography, dictionaries and the references behind the map.

The atlas contains 106 selected language and variety entries. Language-area polygons are generalized and can overlap. A country reference layer fills the land beneath them; it does not describe ethnicity or uniform language use.

The Kurdish ranges include published Kurmanji and Sorani traditional-area supplements with a 1750 reference epoch. They show generalized historical ranges, not a current speaker census.

Aramaic labels distinguish Maaloula Western Neo-Aramaic, Assyrian Neo-Aramaic and Turoyo. Mandaic is a literary/liturgical reference near Basra. Where no suitable language-area polygon is documented, a location label is used.

Canarian tener? is a disputed historical report attributed to La Palma. The question mark is essential: this is not a secure reconstruction, and no relation to mainland Amazigh adfel is asserted. The island fill is a historical reference rather than a surviving speech area.

    Contemporary speaker-area polygons; source atlas published in 2007, digitized dataset version 2.0. CC BY 4.0

    Dataset repository · Dataset DOI · Exact source GeoJSON

  2. Carling, Gerd & Jost Gippert (eds.) 2025. DiACL/TITUS Polygon Archive. Frankfurt am Main: Goethe University.

    Traditional areas for Catalan, Occitan, Cornish, Crimean Tatar, Northern Kurdish and Central Kurdish; reference year 1750, with source timeframes usually 1750–2000. CC BY 4.0

    Dataset repository · Primary resource · Derived dataset DOI

  3. Rantanen, T., Vesakoski, O., Ylikoski, J., & Tolvanen, H. (2021). Geographical database of the Uralic languages (v1.0). Zenodo.

    Traditional Northern Sámi and Veps areas, approximately the widest known at the beginning of the 20th century. CC BY 4.0

    Dataset repository · Original dataset DOI · Derived dataset DOI · Methods paper

  4. Natural Earth 1:50m Admin 0 – Countries

    Complete reference-language land fill underneath language polygons; country boundaries are not linguistic boundaries. Natural Earth public domain

    Source download · Terms of use

  5. Glottolog 5.3: language reference locations

    Reference points for Maaloula Western Neo-Aramaic and Assyrian Neo-Aramaic; locations do not define speaker-area boundaries. CC BY 4.0

    Western Neo-Aramaic · Assyrian Neo-Aramaic

Words and etymologies

Each word and root links to its references. Most comparisons use Wiktionary alongside the dictionaries and institutional resources listed below. Asterisks mark reconstructed forms; uncertain histories are identified in the entry notes.

The Syrian Arabic reading telj and Mesopotamian Arabic thelij were supplied by the map author. Their dictionary link supports the broader Arabic etymology rather than independently verifying those exact regional readings.
